overview: Viva Energy is one of Australia's two listed major liquid fuel suppliers, operating the Geelong Refinery (one of only two remaining Australian oil refineries) alongside a nationwide network of import terminals and distribution infrastructure. It is also Australia's largest convenience retailer, operating roughly 1,280-1,300 fuel and convenience sites under the OTR, Reddy Express (Shell-branded, under licence through 2029) and Liberty Convenience brands, and supplies fuel and specialty products to commercial and industrial (C&I) customers across aviation, mining, defence, marine and transport sectors. Over 15,000 people work across its three segments: Convenience & Mobility (C&M), Commercial & Industrial (C&I), and Energy & Infrastructure (E&I).

business_model.summary: Viva makes money from three distinct but integrated segments: (1) C&M - retail fuel and convenience/food sales through owned/licensed sites, a volume-and-margin business increasingly weighted toward higher-margin convenience and QSR sales; (2) C&I - wholesale/contracted supply of fuel, lubricants, bitumen and specialty products to large corporate, government and industrial customers, generally sticky, relationship-driven and high-retention (top 50 customers average >15 years tenure); (3) E&I - refining crude oil into fuel products at Geelong plus importing/distributing fuel, with earnings driven by the Geelong Refining Margin (GRM) and supported by a Federal Government Fuel Security Services Payment (FSSP) when margins fall below a threshold. Revenue is largely transactional/volume-based (fuel is a low-margin, high-turnover commodity) rather than recurring in a subscription sense, though C&I has long-duration contracts and C&M benefits from habitual/loyalty-driven customer visits (Flybuys, 4cpl dockets with Coles).

revenue_streams.name: Commercial & Industrial (C&I)
revenue_streams.note: Largest EBITDA contributor in FY2025 ($460.5M of $700.9M Group EBITDA RC, ~66%); record fuel sales volumes of 11.8 billion litres

revenue_streams.name: Convenience & Mobility (C&M)
revenue_streams.note: FY2025 EBITDA (RC) $197.4M, down from $231.2M in FY2024 due to integration costs and soft consumer demand; improved materially in 2H2025 and 1H2026 ($138.7M vs $74.4M pcp)

revenue_streams.name: Energy & Infrastructure (E&I) / Refining
revenue_streams.note: FY2025 EBITDA (RC) $93.0M; surged to $353.7M in 1H2026 alone on elevated regional refining margins (GRM averaged US$21.1/bbl vs US$8.2/bbl pcp) driven by Middle East supply disruption

business_model.customer_type: Mixed B2C (retail fuel/convenience motorists via ~1,280+ sites) and B2B/enterprise (aviation, mining, defence, marine, transport, wholesale - C&I's top 50 customers average 15+ years tenure)
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% Australia-domiciled operations; Geelong Refinery (Victoria) supplies >50% of Victoria's fuel needs and >10% of national fuel requirements; national retail and C&I network across all states and territories

competitive_position.market_position: One of Australia's two vertically integrated major fuel companies (alongside Ampol) and one of only two domestic refinery operators; largest convenience retail network in the country by site count following the Coles Express, OTR and Liberty Convenience acquisitions/consolidation. Market share estimates for retail fuel vary widely across sources (low-20s percent range) and are not reliably confirmed.

moat_factors.description: Geelong is one of only two remaining Australian refineries; high barriers to new entry (permitting, capital intensity, environmental approvals) and government support via the FSSP underpin its position in fuel security.
Owns/operates terminals, depots, pipelines and import infrastructure nationwide, critical for reliable supply to C&I customers (aviation, defence, mining, marine) who value continuity over price.

~1,280+ sites under OTR/Reddy Express/Liberty is the largest fuel-and-convenience footprint in Australia, though integration of acquired networks (Coles Express, OTR, Liberty) has been costly and slower than planned.
High switching costs and multi-decade relationships with large industrial/government/aviation customers underpin resilient, diversified C&I earnings.
Reddy Express network carries the Shell brand/fuel under licence through 2029, lending brand trust, but this is a third-party dependency, not an owned asset.

weaknesses: Thin, highly cyclical refining margins exposed to global crack spreads, crude price swings and FX, producing volatile E&I earnings (FY2025 E&I EBITDA $93M vs 1H2026 alone $354M)
C&M integration execution has underperformed management's own targets for multiple years (below-target EBITDA, cost duplication, slower-than-planned OTR conversions)
Reliance on a single ageing, 120-year-old refining asset (Geelong) creates concentrated operational risk, illustrated by the April 2026 Alkylation unit fire

Dependence on Vitol (largest shareholder, ~29.5%) for crude/product supply under an exclusive agreement up for renewal in 2028, with analysts questioning whether shareholders will approve continued exclusivity
Long-term structural risk from EV adoption and fuel efficiency standards (NVES) eroding gasoline demand

growth_drivers: Completion of major capital programs (ULSG plant, ERP systems, Liberty Convenience full acquisition) frees up capital for the next phase of the retail strategy and shareholder returns
Continued OTR network expansion/conversions from Reddy Express and Liberty formats, with loyalty (Flybuys) and digital integration expected to lift basket size and traffic

C&I diversification into new energy solutions - renewable diesel (RD), Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), hydrogen refuelling, and biofuel supply to miners/defence - as a hedge against hydrocarbon demand decline
New Karratha lubricants/grease facility (A$25M, opened Oct 2025) and other speciality product expansion (bitumen, polypropylene, Avgas) where Viva is often the sole domestic manufacturer
Potential New Zealand expansion - reported interest in ExxonMobil's NZ service station network
Low Carbon Liquid Fuels (LCLF) manufacturing pilot at Geelong (co-processing used cooking oil, tyre/plastic pyrolysis oil) positioning the refinery for a multi-decade energy transition role
Unattended/self-service store format conversions (25-30 planned FY2026) to improve convenience margins and labour costs
Elevated regional refining margins in 2026 (Middle East-driven supply disruption) materially lifting near-term E&I earnings and cash generation, accelerating deleveraging

business.description: Multi-year retail integration (Coles Express, OTR, Liberty) has repeatedly missed internal targets; CEO and former C&M CEO forewent FY2025 STI and 2023-2025 LTI vesting was nil for executives, reflecting Board's own dissatisfaction with delivery.
Geelong Refinery outages (e.g., April 2026 Alkylation unit fire, January 2025 lightning-induced shutdown, periodic turnarounds) materially affect E&I output and Group earnings.
Ongoing criminal activity and threatening incidents at convenience sites nationwide; company is engaging police/government but risk to staff safety and reputation persists.

EV uptake, the New Vehicle Efficiency Standard (NVES, first performance period 2026), and improving fuel efficiency are expected to erode gasoline demand over the medium-to-long term, though current financial impact is not material.

financial.description: Net debt was $2.1bn at FY2025-end (leverage 3.0x, down from peak 3.2x at 1H2025); reduced to $1.72bn by 1H2026 aided by strong cash generation, but still a meaningful leverage overhang.
Crude oil/feedstock purchased in USD while products sold predominantly in AUD; AUD/USD swings affect margins despite a hedging program.
Historical-cost accounting produces large swings in statutory profit from inventory valuation (e.g., FY2025 statutory net loss of $421.1M vs RC profit of $183.6M) that can confuse headline results.

regulatory.description: The FSSP mechanism, which supports refining economics when margins are low, is currently under government review/renegotiation; outcome uncertain.
Geelong Refinery accounts for 98% of Group Scope 1 emissions and is subject to Australia's Safeguard Mechanism; compliance costs could rise as policy tightens.

New Ultra-Low Sulphur Gasoline standards took effect 15 December 2025; Viva's $400M ULSG investment (incl. $150M government contribution) positions it to comply and benefit from local refining margin strength.

ACCC conditional clearance of Ampol's ~$1.1bn EG Australia acquisition (41-site divestiture) signals active regulatory attention to fuel retail concentration, which could extend to Viva's own market position over time.

macro.description: Geelong Refining Margin (GRM) is the single largest swing factor in Group earnings - from US$8.2/bbl (1H2025) to US$21.1/bbl (1H2026) - driven by global refining capacity, freight costs and geopolitical supply disruptions (notably the Middle East/Iran conflict in 2026); this tailwind is expected to moderate in 2H2026.

Middle East conflict in 2026 disrupted crude/product flows, lifting regional refining margins and C&I hedging gains; while a tailwind to date, continued or escalating disruption carries both upside and downside risk to supply security and costs.
Cost-of-living pressures and illicit tobacco trade have weighed on convenience store traffic and non-fuel sales (tobacco sales -16.8% YoY in 1H2026).

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Australian fuel refining is a scarce, strategically important but structurally challenged industry (only two refineries remain nationally); convenience retail is consolidating around two major vertically-integrated players (Viva and Ampol) following Coles Express/OTR and EG Australia/Ampol deals. Near-term (2026) refining margins have been unusually strong due to global supply disruption; medium-to-long-term outlook faces secular headwinds from EV adoption and fuel efficiency standards, partially offset by low-carbon liquid fuel (SAF, renewable diesel) opportunities.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High in the E&I/refining segment (margin-driven, linked to global crack spreads and crude price cycles); moderate in C&M (consumer discretionary-linked convenience sales, relatively defensive fuel volumes); low-moderate in C&I (diversified industrial end-markets with long contracts provide earnings resilience).
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - meaningful net debt (~$1.7-2.1bn) and large lease liabilities (~$3.6bn) mean financing costs are sensitive to rates, though covenant headroom is currently ample.
key_input_costs: Labour costs across retail and refinery operations

recent_developments.event: Fire in the Alkylation unit at Geelong Refinery (15 April 2026) disrupted production during a period of elevated margins; refinery operated at reduced rates (petrol ~60%, diesel/jet ~80%) before recovering; RCCU and associated units restarted in June 2026; insurance/business interruption discussions ongoing.

1H2026 results: EBITDA (RC) of $774.4M vs $304.9M pcp, driven by Geelong Refining Margin surge to US$21.1/bbl (from US$8.2/bbl) amid Middle East conflict-driven supply disruption; net debt reduced to $1.72bn from $2.07bn at FY2025-end; interim dividend raised to 7.73 cents (fully franked) from 2.83 cents pcp.

Trading update flagged H1 2026 EBITDA guidance of $770-780 million, more than double the prior year, attributed to geopolitical oil market turmoil; reaffirmed FY2026 capex guidance of approximately $350-400 million.

New Ultra-Low Sulphur Gasoline (ULSG) fuel specification standards came into effect in Australia (15 Dec 2025); Viva's $400M ULSG plant investment (incl. $150M Australian Government contribution) commissioned ahead of the deadline.
Completed acquisition of the remaining 50% stake in Liberty Convenience, bringing the full brand into the C&M portfolio (95 stores) and lifting the national convenience network to over 1,280 stores.
Board renewal: Chair Robert Hill retired (1 March 2026) after ~10 years, succeeded by Sarah Ryan; new Non-Executive Directors John Joyce, Mark Chung and Alistair Bell appointed through the period.
CEO of Convenience & Mobility, Jevan Bouzo, ceased as KMP; interim leadership installed pending a permanent replacement starting in 2026, reflecting ongoing scrutiny of C&M execution.
Viva Energy reportedly evaluating a bid for ExxonMobil's New Zealand service station network, signalling potential geographic expansion beyond Australia.
Macquarie analysts flagged that Viva's exclusive fuel supply agreement with largest shareholder Vitol (renewal due 2028) may face shareholder pushback on continued exclusivity terms.

guidance.as_of: 1H2026 Results / Trading Update (25 August 2026, trading update 28 July 2026)

items.notes: Reaffirmed at 1H2026 results following completion of major capital programs (ULSG, ERP); sharply down from elevated FY2025 investment phase.

items.target: $770-780 million (H1 2026 actual pre-announced via trading update)
items.notes: Actual 1H2026 EBITDA (RC) came in at $774.4M, within the pre-announced range; driven by exceptional refining margins from Middle East-related supply disruption; management and analysts (Ord Minnett) expect these drivers to fade in 2H2026, with H2 EBITDA likely closer to CY2025 levels.

items.target: 20-25 new OTR stores and 10-15 Reddy Express-to-OTR/Liberty conversions
items.vs_prior: lowered vs the 40-60 store openings/conversions flagged in the FY2025 annual report (Feb 2026)
items.notes: Store rollout plan scaled back and prioritised toward high-return projects amid a challenging consumer/retail environment; also targeting 25-30 store conversions to unattended/self-service format.

items.target: Expected to remain strong through the remainder of FY2026 (qualitative; July 2026 GRM was US$20.7/bbl)
items.vs_prior: no formal numeric guidance issued; analyst estimates range ~US$14.60-20/bbl for 2H26
items.notes: Management says margins are supported near-term but some hedging/supply benefits that lifted 1H2026 are not expected to recur at the same strength in 2H2026.

CEO flagged continued synergy/margin benefits and new store openings but said growth would be modest due to the operating environment and temporary cost duplication from the ongoing OTR/Reddy Express/Liberty integration.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Scott Wyatt said the Group enters 2026 'with strong momentum, a clearer strategic path and a more integrated platform,' with 2026 priorities on executing the next phase of the retail strategy (loyalty/digital integration, own convenience supply chain) and renegotiating the FSSP refining support mechanism with the Federal Government. Chair (outgoing) Robert Hill said major capital programs are now complete and the Board is confident the Company can strengthen its balance sheet and return cash to shareholders via operating cashflow. At 1H2026, management highlighted that elevated refining margins from Middle East-related disruption were a temporary tailwind, not expected to persist at the same magnitude into 2H2026.

bull_case: Rare, hard-to-replicate asset base: one of only two Australian refineries plus the country's largest convenience network, both difficult and capital-intensive to replicate, supported by government fuel-security policy (FSSP)

Major capital investment cycle (ULSG plant, ERP systems, Liberty/OTR integration) is now largely complete, freeing cash flow for deleveraging and shareholder returns just as refining margins have turned sharply favourable in 2026
Diversified, resilient C&I segment delivering record volumes and consistent EBITDA growth, underpinned by multi-decade customer relationships across aviation, defence, mining and marine

2026 refining margin windfall (GRM more than doubled YoY) is rapidly reducing net debt and leverage (3.0x down toward lower levels), improving balance sheet flexibility and dividend capacity (interim dividend nearly tripled YoY)

Optionality in low-carbon liquid fuels (SAF, renewable diesel, hydrogen) and speciality products (bitumen, polypropylene, lubricants, Avgas) where Viva already holds domestic manufacturing monopolies, providing a multi-decade transition pathway for the refinery
bear_case: C&M segment has persistently underperformed management's own targets for several years, with cost duplication, slower-than-planned conversions, and leadership turnover (CEO C&M departure) suggesting execution risk remains elevated

E&I/refining earnings are extremely volatile and currently inflated by a geopolitical (Middle East conflict) supply shock; management and analysts expect the refining margin tailwind to fade materially in 2H2026 and beyond, risking a sharp earnings reversion

Single-site refinery concentration risk crystallised in the April 2026 Alkylation unit fire, demonstrating vulnerability to unplanned outages that can remove a large share of Group earnings with little warning
Structural, multi-decade demand risk from EV adoption and fuel efficiency standards (NVES) could gradually erode the core hydrocarbon fuel business that still generates the bulk of volumes

Key dependency on Vitol (largest shareholder, ~29.5% stake) for crude/product supply under an exclusive arrangement up for renewal in 2028, with analysts questioning whether shareholders will approve continued exclusivity on current terms, creating a multi-year governance/strategic overhang
